column1: # Line-count tolerance for a ported file, over and above the 5% the rule allows every
# file.  The line count is a crude drift signal - the per-function token check is the real
# guard - so a file whose ledger records a *structural* expansion of C's text (a form Rust
# cannot spell in the same number of physical lines) declares its tolerance here with the
# reason, instead of losing the readability of the port to fit 5%.  One
# `<stem>\t<tolerance>\t<reason>` per line; the check uses max(0.05, tolerance).

column3: C 284 vs the port's 383: C's three `label`s (`onedigit:`, `twodigit:`) and its four `FALLTHROUGH`s into the `%d`/`%3`/`%2` chain must become one shared statement sequence with an entry stage (PORTING.md 2.2), which costs physical lines the C text does not have

C 1435 vs the port's 1534: the three `bool_bf` bits of every itree_node are read and written through the ITREE_* masks instead of `node->red` (extra expression per access, PORTING.md 1.3), the iterator's `switch` becomes a `match` with braced arms, and the `while ((next = ...))` conditions become loops with an explicit test

C 874 vs the port's 988 (13.0%): the two CONSIDER macros become helper functions plus one `if let Some (value) = … { return value; }` per use site (twelve of them), the `#ifdef MARKER_DEBUG` arm keeps its three functions behind `#[cfg (feature = "marker_debug")]`, and the eight `DEFUN!` bodies carry the docstring in the invocation

C 56 vs the port's 71: each of the three dead `#if !HAVE_*` arms is kept as a `#[cfg (feature = "…")]` block (P-51), which costs the attribute, the braces and the comment C does not have, and the two `#define`s are constants rather than preprocessor lines
C 101 vs the port's 88: the dead arms are `#[cfg (feature = "…")]` blocks and the two `#define`s are constants; the frozen body keeps C's empty `if (n == 0)` block
C 933 vs the port's 983 (5.4%): the two shared-body entry stages (C's `goto have_prefix_arg` and the two `FALLTHROUGH`s) and the invalid-letter helper each cost a few lines the C text does not have

C 351 vs the port's 423 (20.5%): the 32 arms whose signal this target does not define carry the P-51 comment and the `#[cfg (feature = "signal_…")]` line that keep C's text, and the match's closing braces cost the arms C's `case …:` one-liners do not

C 55 vs the port's 76 (38.2%): a 55-line reference cannot absorb the port's standard fixed costs - the `// femacs:` note, the `#![allow (…)]` block and the unit's own `tparm` declaration block (C declares tparm on one line, the port needs an `unsafe extern` block) - while the arms, statements and objects all match one for one

C 154 vs the port's ~87: the Windows arm's three items are kept as `#[cfg (feature = "windows_native")]` text, each adding an attribute line, while the live body is five lines that C reaches through four nested `#if` levels
